newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Economic impact from S.Korean strikes seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Economic impact from S.Korean strikes seen limited.

text.p: Despite the threat of the biggest ever strike in South Korea, and international criticism of a new labour law, worker unrest is expected to have only a limited impact on the economy, analysts said on Thursday.
They said the political nature of the strikes and a public consensus on the need for labour reform would pressure many unionists to return to work.

"The way the legislation was conducted will leave some uncertainty in labour-management relations but I don't see any devastating effect on the economy from union struggles," said economist Shin Hu-shig of Daewoo Research Institute.
"If the strikes fizzle out in a few weeks, which I think will happen, the damage could be recouped," he said.
South Korea's largest union umbrella body called on Thursday for the biggest strike in the country's history in protest at a new labour law.
The law will end decades of near-total job security by allowing employers to lay off workers and hire temporary workers to replace strikers.
On Wednesday, the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) said the law compounded existing violations of international labour law in the country.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions, with 1.2 million members, said a two-day strike would begin next Tuesday.
City buses around the nation would be halted along with subway lines in Seoul under its control. Hospitals, banks, hotels, taxis, and many state firms would be affected, it said.
If most federation members respond it will be the largest stoppage in terms of the number of participants since 1989, when about 400,000 workers joined in.
The federation will join strikes now under way by members of a smaller union body, the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which has half a million workers.
The confederation has ordered all-out stoppages from next Wednesday unless the government scraps the new law. The government has rejected a backdown.
An Asian diplomat said the present strike action differed from the 1989 protests.
"...the 1989 strike continued for nearly five months and the nature of protests was drastically different from those of the current industrial action," the diplomat said.
In the earlier round of industrial unrest, workers set fire to public facilities and used bulldozers and cranes to confront police in protests for higher pay and improved working conditions.
The current strikes have been largely peaceful.
"It's more politicking and posturing than it is a real attempt to repeal certain provisions of the law," said Richard Samuelson, head of research at SG Warburg Securities in Seoul.
Officials said on Thursday the latest strikes have cost the country 1.62 trillion won ($1.92 billion) in lost production.
A Daewoo Research Institute report said this compared with about 4.2 trillion won of lost production in 1989.

It said the economic growth rate would slow to 5.5 percent this year from an original forecast of 5.9 percent if production losses matched those of 1989. Consumer prices would rise by 5.3 percent instead of 4.9 percent.
"I personally don't think this will be the case but even if we have that scenario it would not be a disaster," Shin said. "High levels of inventory would also cushion the effect."
Lee Sang-deuk, chairman of the ruling New Korea Party's policy committee, said he saw no coordinated action by the two main umbrella union bodies, which guard their turf jealously.
Lee said workers fully understood average annual wages rises of 16 percent in the past decade had outstripped productivity increases.
"They also know the Korean economy is in trouble. We believe the vast majority of workers will go back to work in the near future," he said. ($=845 won)
